findings.where: First screen, the blue field behind everything (desktop and phone): the diagonal hatching across the whole field, and the large ghost 'PPP' letters behind the heading (on the phone, cropped 'PP' fragments to the right of the heading)
findings.fault: The direction is meant to be one flat field of house blue, and the tile's own Texture panel says 'No texture: one flat field, no grain and no gradient'. The hero instead has a busy striped ground plus a watermark of letters. The style tile misdescribes its own hero. The hatching reads as a drafting or blueprint borrowing, and the ghost letters add a novelty layer behind Mark's line that blurs the heading's letter shapes. On the phone the cropped letters are just stray shapes.
findings.who_objects: The founder, who judges the first screen first and asked for a quiet ground and serious type ('one soft ground at low contrast', 'at most one borrowed detail', nothing 'in-your-face techy'). Mark, whose sentence has to compete with a pattern. A bank officer, who reads the stripes and watermark as template decoration and not as a refined advisor's page.

findings.where: First screen, the row of five outlined pills under the lead (PPP Law, Infrastructure, Development banks, Governments, Risk allocation), desktop and phone
findings.fault: These are static text, but they are drawn as outlined capsules in the same white-on-blue as the one real action beside them, so they look like filter chips or buttons. A visitor who clicks 'PPP Law' expecting his PPP work gets nothing. They also add five more boxed things to a first screen that should hold one message and one action, which weakens the email button's claim to be the action.
findings.who_objects: A development-bank visitor who taps a topic to see Mark's work on it and finds a dead control. The founder, who asked for one action on the first screen.

findings.where: Article specimen: the 'Streamlining the PPP Process…' link and the list bullets (desktop and phone)
findings.fault: The link and bullets are set in a red-orange that appears nowhere else. It contradicts the tile's own palette ('Four colours and no accent… links and the action' in house blue), the house colours the founder asked for, and the 'Play again' link a few lines away, which is house blue. Two link colours on one page also make it unclear what a link looks like.
findings.who_objects: The founder, who asked for every tile to be built in or around #0070C0 and #404040 and for at most one accent. Angélique, who needs one link style to apply when she adds articles.

findings.where: Article specimen: the image caption, the subhead 'So, what are the key ‘chapter topics’?' and the three-item list (desktop and phone)
findings.fault: The vertical rhythm breaks at exactly the parts the brief asked this specimen to prove. The caption is jammed against the photo above and the subhead below with almost no space, so the caption reads as part of the subhead. The list is set much tighter than the 19/30 body text, and its wrapped lines nearly touch (very visible on the phone). The list then runs straight into the divider and PDF row.
findings.who_objects: The founder and round 1's critics, who made 'the look must survive Angélique's content… type sits on a rhythm that holds when she adds an image, a caption, a list or a subhead' a requirement. Every reader of a long article, who loses the separation between caption, heading and text.

findings.where: Article specimen: the subhead 'So, what are the key ‘chapter topics’?' against the article title 'The World's Best Public-Private Partnership Law'
findings.fault: The subhead is set at about the same size and weight as the article title, so a section heading competes with the page's title. A reader skimming cannot tell where the article starts and where a section starts.
findings.who_objects: A reader of Mark's articles scanning a long piece, and Angélique, who needs a subhead style clearly below the title.

findings.where: Article specimen: the lone PDF row under the list ('Streamlining the PPP Process… · Lecture · 23 April 2026 · PDF')
findings.fault: The one publication row has no heading and sits straight under the article's list, separated only by a hairline. It reads as a stray footnote of the article, not as the start of Mark's list of papers and talks, which the research calls 'the product'.
findings.who_objects: A procurement reader looking for Mark's lectures and papers as evidence of his work, who would not see this as a body of publications.

findings.where: Nav lockup, top left (desktop and phone): the white aqueduct mark with 'MMM INFRA', then a rule, then 'Mark M. Moseley' and the firm line
findings.fault: The mark comes first and outweighs the name. 'Mark M. Moseley' is set small, at about the size of a nav label, so the firm's mark leads and his name follows. The brief asks for the opposite.
findings.who_objects: The founder, whose personal-advisor test requires 'his name leads, with the logo beside it' and rejects 'the firm is the brand'.

findings.where: Phone first screen: the full-width portrait placed before the heading
findings.fault: At 390 px the portrait fills the first phone screen. Mark's line starts only at its bottom edge, and the lead and the email action fall to the second screen, so a phone visitor's first view is a photo and a nav with no message and no way to reach him.
findings.who_objects: A visitor who opens the link from LinkedIn on a phone, who sees a headshot but not what Mark does or how to write to him without scrolling.

findings.where: Article specimen title 'The World's Best…' against the subhead's ‘chapter topics’
findings.fault: The title's apostrophe in 'World's' renders as a straight mark, while the subhead uses curly quotes. The mismatch is visible at display size.
findings.who_objects: A careful reader, and Mark, whose legal-journal register depends on finished typesetting.
